title: When the House Breaks
premise: Folklorist Silas Ashgrove returns to Hollowmere to record a lullaby the villagers refuse to sing twice, only to find his childhood imaginary friend, Wren, waiting on his porch — unchanged after thirty years. Wren reveals that every child who learned the song's first two verses was taken by something beneath the house on Ash Hill, and Silas was the one who got away because Wren took his place in the singing. As neighbors begin vanishing again and the song resurfaces in the mouths of children who never heard it, Silas must recover the forbidden third verse from the village's oldest survivor without ever singing along himself. In the end, Silas learns the verse is not an invitation but a binding: sung in full by someone who refuses to join the chorus, it locks the thing beneath the hill away for another generation — and Wren, finally released from his vigil, fades with the last note.
about_author: Vesper Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist of regional ballads who spent a decade collecting songs in remote English villages before turning to fiction. They write horror rooted in folk tradition, where old melodies carry older debts.

chapters.title: The Song Nobody Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Silas arrives in Hollowmere with recording equipment and fifteen years of rationalizations, chasing a lullaby mentioned in a dead collector's notes. An innkeeper's wife hums four bars, then goes white and stops. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professional curiosity; the reader feels the village's fear before Silas admits his own.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: At the crumbling Ashgrove cottage, Silas finds Wren — his childhood imaginary friend — sitting on the porch steps, exactly eight years old, unchanged. Wren says only: 'You're late. It started again.' POV: Silas. Emotional beat: uncanny dread braided with aching tenderness; the return of belonging in its most impossible form.

chapters.title: What the Children Remember
chapters.summary: Silas interviews villagers whose grown children all recall the same melody no parent taught them. A schoolteacher shows him a child's drawing of a door beneath a hill. POV: Silas, with a brief interlude from the schoolteacher's diary. Emotional beat: mounting dread as patterns emerge; the comfort of community curdles into complicity.

chapters.title: The First Verse
chapters.summary: Wren leads Silas to the well behind the cottage and sings the first verse, warning him never to answer it. That night, Silas dreams of descending stairs inside Ash Hill and wakes with dirt under his fingernails. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: temptation and terror entwined; the song wants him, and part of him wants it back.

chapters.title: Margaret Under the Yew
chapters.summary: Silas seeks Margaret Fenwick, ninety-one, the last person who heard the whole song sung. She lives warded behind iron nails and salt, and she tells him the second verse before slamming the door: 'Never the third. The third is how it listens back.' POV: Silas. Emotional beat: grim resolve; justice here was never legal, only practical and cruel.

chapters.title: A Chorus of Small Voices
chapters.summary: Children across the village begin singing the second verse at play, though none admit learning it. A boy goes missing overnight; searchers find his shoes neatly placed at the hill's base. POV: alternating between Silas and the missing boy's mother, Edie. Emotional beat: grief and guilt; the village's found-family bonds strain against their shared secret.

chapters.title: What Wren Gave Up
chapters.summary: Wren confesses he was once a real child of Hollowmere, taken in 1931, who bargained to become Silas's guardian instead of the thing's chorus. His protection ends when Silas learns the third verse. POV: Wren — the book's only chapter outside Silas's head. Emotional beat: devastating sacrifice revealed; love as a debt paid across decades.

chapters.title: The Door Beneath the Hill
chapters.summary: Edie's son is still alive below — Wren can feel him. Silas descends into Ash Hill through the barrow door, hearing the full three verses sung by generations of taken children, and nearly joins them when the melody hooks his breath. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: climax of dread; the seduction of surrender versus the stubborn refusal to belong on the thing's terms.

chapters.title: The Third Verse
chapters.summary: In the dark, Silas makes Margaret teach him the third verse over a tinny phone call, memorizing it without voicing a syllable. He speaks — never sings — the binding words at the threshold while the chorus screams, and the door seals. The boy walks out into dawn. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: triumphant defiance; justice delivered outside any law, by a man who refused the terms of belonging.

chapters.title: Unchanged No Longer
chapters.summary: The village slowly exhales; Edie takes Silas in like family, and he begins recording the songs they'll now sing twice. On the porch, Wren ages a year with each sunset until, freed, he becomes an old man for one final evening and thanks Silas before dissolving into birdsong. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; found family earned, belonging chosen rather than taken, and grief that is also gratitude.
